articles.title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index
articles.content: Google DeepMind just released Gemini 4 Neon. Gemini 4 Neon is a reasoning model that sits between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It targets coding agents, knowledge work and science workflows. The developer pitch is near-frontier scores at a lower cost per task. Pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. TL;DR Size: 1M-token unified context, 64K default output, up to 1M via background long decode. Runs on: Google-hosted only. Closed weights, so no local GPU, quantized or edge builds. Performance: 61 on the AA Intelligence Index, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (59) and GPT-6.2 Sol (57). Best: 95.2% on GraphWalks (256K to 1M context), vs 80.1% for GPT-6.2 Sol. Worst: 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 47.3%. Bottom line: Best: leads long-context and agentic coding at $3/$15. Worst: closed, self-reported, pricier per token than GPT-6.2 Sol. What is Gemini 4 Neon? Neon is the middle model in the Gemini 4 family. Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon projects. Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon balances depth and efficiency between the two. As per the model card, Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count or architecture. Inputs cover text, images, audio and video. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. How does Neon work inside agent workflows? Neon exposes multiple thinking levels. High is the default. xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and makes fewer redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity, Neon can act as an orchestrator. It directs parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller subtasks. How does Gemini 4 Neon perform on benchmarks? Google compares Neon against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. All scores below are reported by Google, not independently reproduced. Coding: #1 on the AA Coding Agent Index at 58.6. SWE-sweep with provider harness hits 39.0%, vs 10.1% for Opus 5.5. Knowledge work: 56.3% on Zapier AutomationBench, vs 42.5% for Opus 5.5. 75.8% on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1. Science and reasoning: 84.0% on RiemannBench, 70.5% on Terminal-Bench-Science and 71.3% on HLE-Diamond. Long context: 95.2% on GraphWalks, vs 66.8% for Opus 5.5. Cyber: 90.5% on SEC-bench Pro, 70.7% on CWE-Bench v2 and 51.3% on WebExploitBench v1.2. Neon does not win every row. Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (47.3% vs 46.2%). GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography (75.1% vs 73.5%). On the Vals Index, Neon scores 70.9% and ranks #2. On the Agent Arena index it also ranks #2, with a score of 1336. &&& What does Gemini 4 Neon cost? Neon lists at $3 input, $0.15 cached input and $15 output per 1M tokens. Google says Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It also claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task vs rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. Those are per-task claims, not per-token prices. GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10. Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. Gemini 4 Carbon is $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20. Where can developers use Gemini 4 Neon? Gemini API paid tier, via Google AI Studio and Android Studio Gemini for business, via API and the model dropdown Google Antigravity, for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers The Gemini app, for Pro and Ultra subscribers What do the safety numbers show? Neon runs on the Gemini 4 safety and security stack. Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite. It passes 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation. It shows a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its 2.45% shortcut rate on a coding cheating test is the lowest of any Gemini 4 model. AA scores for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol match Artificial Analysis. Key Takeaways Neon sits between Carbon and Hydrogen, priced at $3/$15 per 1M tokens. Scores 61 on AA Intelligence Index, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index. Biggest lead: 95.2% on GraphWalks long-context recall. Trails Opus 5.5 on Terminal-bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0. Closed and API-only, with Google-reported benchmarks. Check out the launch post and the model card. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. articles.title: GPT-5.6
articles.content:
July 9, 2026

More intelligence from every token, stronger performance per dollar, and more capability on demand for your hardest work.

Learn about OpenAI’s latest model:

Update on August 21, 2026:OpenAI dropped the API and credit pricing of GPT‑5.6 Sol by over 20% for the next 3 months.

Update on July 30, 2026:OpenAI reduced the price of GPT‑5.6 Luna by 80% and GPT‑5.6 Terra by 20%.Learn more here.

We’re launching the GPT‑5.6 family of models for general availability following ourlimited preview⁠: our new flagship,Sol, alongsideTerra, a balanced model for everyday work, andLuna, our most cost-efficient model.

GPT‑5.6 Sol sets a new standard for both intelligence and efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art results across coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity, and science while outperforming previous and competing frontier models with fewer tokens and at lower estimated cost. The result is stronger performance per dollar: more successful work for the same spend, or comparable results at a lower total cost. We also introduce a new way to accelerate the most demanding work:ultrais our highest-capability setting, coordinating multiple agents across parallel workstreams to finish complex tasks faster. Stronger computer use and design judgment make GPT‑5.6 Sol our most polished collaborator yet, helping it inspect, refine, and deliver ready-to-use results.

We trained GPT‑5.6 to get more useful work from every token. OnAgents’ Last Exam⁠(opens in a new window), an evaluation of long-running professional workflows across 55 fields, GPT‑5.6 Sol sets a new high of 53.6, eclipsing Claude Fable 5 (adaptive reasoning) by 13.1 points. Even at medium reasoning, it beats Fable 5 by 11.4 points at roughly one-quarter the estimated cost. That efficiency extends to smaller models, which are essential to making intelligence more abundant and affordable: GPT‑5.6 Terra and GPT‑5.6 Luna outperform Fable 5 at around one-sixteenth the cost. On theArtificial Analysis Intelligence Index⁠(opens in a new window), a broad measure of intelligence spanning agentic work, coding, scientific reasoning, and general capabilities, GPT‑5.6 Sol with max reasoning comes within one point of Fable 5 while completing tasks in 61% less time at roughly half the estimated cost.

GPT‑5.6 launches with our most robust safeguards to date, designed to be resilient against determined and adaptive misuse without broadly limiting legitimate work. Before general availability, we put the models and safeguards through our most extensive evaluation period yet, combining human red teaming with large-scale automated testing. During the preview, we worked closely with expert organizations and with trusted partners to pressure-test defenses and strengthen safeguards before broader launch. The resulting system layers protections trained into the model with real-time checks, monitoring, and access calibrated to trust and risk.

GPT‑5.6 Sol is our best coding model yet. On theArtificial Analysis Coding Agent Index,GPT‑5.6 Sol with max reasoning sets a new state of the art at 80, 2.8 points above Fable 5, while using less than half the output tokens, taking less than half the time, and costing about one-third less. That advantage extends across the family: Terra performs just above Fable 5, while Luna outperforms Opus 4.8; each does so in roughly one-third of the time, with about half as many output tokens, and at approximately one-quarter the estimated cost. It also sets new state-of-the-art results on Terminal‑Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE, which test complex command-line workflows and long-horizon engineering in real codebases.

GPT‑5.6 can write and run lightweight programs that coordinate tools, process intermediate results, monitor progress, and choose the next action as work unfolds. This lets tool-heavy tasks advance with fewer tokens, fewer model round trips, and less guidance. Instead of requiring developers to script every step or passing every tool response back through the model,Programmatic Tool Calling⁠(opens in a new window)in the Responses API can filter large amounts of intermediate data, retain only what matters, and adapt its workflow along the way.

For problems that reward a greater investment of time and compute, GPT‑5.6 can push beyond this efficient default.maxgives GPT‑5.6 even more time thanxhighto reason and explore alternatives, run checks, and revise its approach.ultragoes further by coordinating four agents in parallel by default, trading higher token use for stronger results and faster time-to-result on demanding tasks. The charts below compare ultra’s default four-agent setup with a one-agent baseline across BrowseComp, SEC-Bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench 2.1; BrowseComp and SEC-Bench Pro also show 16-agent configurations. Across all three evaluations, adding parallel agents shifts the score-latency frontier upward and to the left, reaching stronger results in less time. In the API, developers can build ultra-like experiences using themulti-agent⁠(opens in a new window)beta in the Responses API.4,5,6

GPT‑5.6 delivers a step change in design judgment. With only high-level direction, GPT‑5.6 creates tasteful, ergonomic, and functional interfaces. Its stronger computer-use capabilities let it inspect and refine the rendered result—not just generate the underlying code or content—so it can catch visual and functional issues and apply finishing touches before handing the work back.

GPT‑5.6’s frontend capabilities also turn natural-language requests into polished, interactive explanations and visualizations within ChatGPT Work.

GPT‑5.6delivers better results for professional tasks. It takes messy context from your documents and everyday workflows like Slack, Notion, Microsoft 365, and Google Drive, and converts it into expert-level, shareable artifacts.

GPT‑5.6’s strength on knowledge work shows up in evaluations spanning long-horizon professional analysis, browsing, tool use, and computer use. GPT‑5.6 Sol sets new state-of-the-art results onBrowseCompat 92.2% andOSWorld 2.0at 62.6%; on OSWorld, it surpasses Opus 4.8 while using 85% fewer output tokens. Here, the performance-per-dollar gains extend across the GPT‑5.6 family. Luna nearly matches GPT‑5.5’s peak performance at less than half the estimated cost, while Terra surpasses it at a lower cost.

GPT‑5.6 Sol improves quality in presentations, documents, and spreadsheets,producing outputs that are more polished and accurate. It can create fully editable presentations from scratch, translating a prompt and source material into a coherent visual narrative with strong layouts, hierarchy, and design.

The improvement is especially pronounced when following templates and reference decks.GPT‑5.6 can infer a deck’s design system—layouts, typography, spacing, colors, and recurring content patterns, including rules embedded in the Slide Master—and apply those conventions consistently to new material. In this example, when asked to update numbers based on a reference file, the GPT‑5.5 output is missing key components from the master slide, while GPT‑5.6 follows the reference structure more faithfully.

GPT‑5.6 also creates more visually refined documents and spreadsheets. It follows complex reference formats more faithfully, which is important for repeatable knowledge work activities. It handles equations and financial models with greater precision, and makes better use of typography, spacing, hierarchy, and page or worksheet layout.

Early customers testing GPT‑5.6 saw improvements to knowledge work outputs across domains.

GPT‑5.6 is our strongest cybersecurity model yet, achieving frontier performance with significantly fewer tokens. OnExploitBench2,which measures progress from reaching vulnerable code through arbitrary code execution, it scores 73.5% versus GPT‑5.5’s 47.9% at a comparable output-token budget. OnExploitGym3,which asks agents to turn real-world vulnerabilities into working exploits, it almost doubles GPT‑5.5’s peak pass rate, from 15.1% to 24.9% under the two-hour cap; with six hours, it reaches 33.7%. OnSEC-Bench Pro,which tests proof-of-concept generation on complex software, it scores 71.2% versus GPT‑5.5’s 45.8% at an improved latency.1

GPT‑5.6 supports important defensive tasks such as secure code review, patching, threat modeling, and blue teaming. Qualified individuals and organizations inOpenAI Daybreak’s Trusted Access for Cyber⁠program can access more of its defensive capability through more precise safeguards for verified work in authorized environments, including vulnerability triage and validation, malware analysis, detection engineering, and patch validation.

Individuals canverify their identity and request trusted access⁠(opens in a new window), and organizations canapply⁠for their teams. Individual members will need to enableAdvanced Account Security⁠(opens in a new window)with hardware-backed passkeys by September 1 to retain access to our most cyber-capable frontier models; those who do not will return to default access. Users who do not already have hardware-backed passkeys can receivepreferred pricing⁠(opens in a new window)from our partner, Yubico. We are also taking additional steps to restrict access to high-risk entities and in high-risk jurisdictions.

GPT‑5.6 Sol also shows broad gains acrossscientific research. On life sciences evaluations, GPT‑5.6 demonstrates Pareto improvements over GPT‑5.5 on real-world biology, life science research workflows, and chemistry.

GPT‑5.6 is our strongest model yet for accelerating AI research. Inside OpenAI, researchers use it across the development loop: diagnosing failures, optimizing training systems, running experiments, and interpreting results. We already saw that acceleration and stronger adoption during the internal testing period of GPT‑5.6, as average daily output tokens per active researcher were more than twice the highest level observed for GPT‑5.5.

articles.title: Engineering
articles.content:
November 19, 2026

Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff

The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

1. Pre-Codex.Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we hadCodex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill calledperf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

Find when the slowdown began

Identify the affected requests

Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

We tested and refined theperf-forensicsskill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills likeperf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

Adispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on anenvironment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

The agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

Some work has to wait for a person or a deployment; an agent shouldn’t have to keep running in the meantime. When a task needs to wait, it can subscribe to events like review comments or failed CI checks on a GitHub pull request to get notified when it’s time to pick the work back up.When an incoming event matches the subscription, the task becomes ready again and the dispatch loop can then assign an agent to continue the work.

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow.A performance regression moves through several stages:needs investigation,root caused,fix proposed, andresolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

Active stage: Detected

The Regression Workflow’s steps include finding the root cause, proposing a fix, reviewing and deploying, and verifying recovery.

Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. Theperf-forensicsskill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

Once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. articles.title: 정부, AI 데이터센터 전력 규제 완화…비수도권 50MW 이하 영향평가 면제
articles.content:
정부가 AI 산업의 핵심 인프라인 인공지능 데이터센터(AIDC)의 구축 속도를 높이기 위해 전력계통영향평가 제도를 개선한다.

비수도권에 들어서는 계약전력 50메가와트(MW) 이하 AI 데이터센터는 평가 대상에서 제외하고, AIDC 특구 내 시설에는 전력계통의 기술적 안정성 평가만 적용하고 대규모 AIDC 사업에는 우선 평가 절차를 도입해 인허가와 착공에 걸리는 시간을 줄일 방침이다.

과학기술정보통신부(부총리 겸 장관 배경훈)와 기후에너지환경부(장관 김성환)는 AIDC의 신속한 구축을 지원하기 위해 전력계통영향평가 면제 기준과 평가 절차를 개선하는 방안을 마련하고, 관련 시행령 입법예고와 후속 제도 정비를 추진한다고 20일 밝혔다.

전력계통영향평가는 대규모 전력 사용시설이 지역 전력망에 미치는 영향을 사전에 검토하는 제도다. AIDC는 고성능 그래픽처리장치(GPU)와 서버를 대규모로 운영하는 특성상 상당한 전력을 지속적으로 사용하기 때문에 전력 공급 여건과 계통 안정성 확보가 중요한 입지 조건으로 꼽힌다.

정부는 2027년 3월 10일 시행 예정인 '인공지능 데이터센터 산업 진흥에 관한 특별법'에 맞춰 비수도권 AIDC의 전력계통영향평가 면제 기준을 계약전력 50MW 이하로 정했다. 적용 대상은 비수도권에서 신축하거나 증축·전환하는 AIDC다. 해당 시설이 계약전력 기준을 충족하면 전력계통영향평가를 받지 않아도 된다.

정부는 업계의 규제 완화 요구와 대규모 전력 수요가 지역 전력망에 미치는 영향을 함께 고려해 면제 기준을 설정했다고 설명했다. 특히 면제 기준을 100MW로 높이더라도 기가와트(GW)급 메가프로젝트에 해당하는 초대형 AIDC는 대부분 평가 대상에 남는다는 점을 검토했다. 사업자들이 평가 과정에서 기술적 검토보다 비기술적 평가자료를 준비하는 데 상당한 시간을 투입한다는 점도 제도 개선에 반영했다.

이에 따라 정부는 계약전력 50MW 이하 시설의 평가 면제와 별도로 AIDC 특구에 대한 평가 간소화 제도를 도입하기로 했다.

AI 데이터센터 특별법에 따라 지정되는 특구 안의 데이터센터는 전력 사용 규모와 관계없이 전력계통영향평가의 비기술적 항목을 면제받는다. 전력망에 미치는 영향을 확인하는 기술적 평가는 유지한다. 기후부는 '전력계통영향평가 제도 운영에 관한 규정'을 개정해 해당 기준을 반영할 계획이다.

정부는 AIDC 특구와 분산에너지특화지역의 연계도 강화한다. 현행 분산에너지특화지역 가운데 수요유치형 분산특구는 이미 전력계통영향평가의 비기술적 항목을 면제받고 있다. AI 데이터센터 특구에도 유사한 평가 간소화 방식을 적용하면 두 특구 간 제도적 연계가 강화되고, 지역 전력 공급 여건을 고려한 데이터센터 입지 조성에도 도움이 될 것으로 기대된다.

다만 비기술적 평가를 면제하는 과정에서 기술적 평가의 전력 수요 관련 점수 구간은 조정될 수 있다. 평가 절차를 줄이더라도 지역 전력망의 안정성을 확인하는 기능은 유지하겠다는 취지다.

초대형 AIDC 사업에는 평가 순서를 앞당기는 패스트트랙을 적용한다. 정부는 메가프로젝트에 해당하는 AI 데이터센터와 특별법에 따른 인허가 일괄처리를 신청한 AI 데이터센터를 전력 사용 규모와 관계없이 우선 평가하기로 했다.

기후부는 현재 마련 중인 전력계통영향평가 업무 매뉴얼에 우선 평가 규정을 명시할 예정이다. 사업자가 계통 평가를 받기 위해 대기하는 기간을 최소화하고, 인허가 절차와 연계해 착공 일정을 단축하도록 지원한다는 계획이다.

패스트트랙은 평가 자체를 면제하는 제도가 아니라 평가 순서를 우선 배정하는 방식이다. 대규모 전력 수요가 발생하는 AIDC는 필요한 기술적 검토를 거치되 행정적 대기시간을 줄이는 데 초점을 맞췄다. 정부의 제도 개선은 AIDC 구축 과정에서 전력망 접근성과 인허가 일정이 주요 사업 변수로 부상한 상황을 반영한 조치다.

특히 대규모 AI 연산 인프라 확충을 위해서는 데이터센터 건설뿐 아니라 전력 공급 능력과 계통 연결 가능성을 함께 확보해야 한다. 비수도권 시설의 평가 부담을 낮추고 초대형 사업의 심사 절차를 우선 처리하는 방식은 지역 AI 인프라 투자를 촉진하는 정책 수단으로 활용될 전망이다.

과기정통부 류제명 제2차관은 "AI 데이터센터가 적기에 구축될 수 있도록 기후부와 긴밀한 협의를 거쳐 맞춤형 개선 방안을 마련했다"며 "2027년 3월 10일 특별법 시행에 맞춰 개선된 전력계통영향평가 제도가 차질 없이 정착하도록 노력하겠다"고 밝혔다.

기후부 이호현 제2차관은 "전력계통의 안정성을 지키면서 메가프로젝트 등 AI 데이터센터의 신속한 구축을 뒷받침할 수 있도록 고시 개정과 세부 업무 매뉴얼 마련을 조속히 마무리하겠다"고 말했다.

정부가 추진하는 전력계통영향평가 개선은 비수도권 중소·중대형 AI 데이터센터의 규제 부담을 줄이는 동시에 초대형 AI 인프라 사업의 행정 처리 속도를 높이는 데 의미가 있다. 향후 제도 시행의 실효성은 시행령과 고시 개정 일정, 특구 지정 기준, 우선 평가 절차의 구체화뿐 아니라 실제 전력 공급 능력과 송전망 확충 여건에 따라 좌우될 것으로 보인다.
articles.summary: 정부가 비수도권에서 신축·증축·전환하는 계약전력 50MW 이하 AI 데이터센터를 전력계통영향평가 대상에서 제외하는 제도 개선을 추진한다. AI 데이터센터 특구에서는 전력 규모와 관계없이 비기술적 평가를 면제하되 전력망 안정성에 관한 기술적 검토는 유지하고, 초대형 사업에는 우선 평가 절차를 적용할 계획이다. 이번 조치는 2027년 3월 10일 시행 예정인 특별법에 맞춘 것으로, 시행령 입법예고와 후속 규정 정비가 남아 있다. 국내 AI 인프라 사업의 인허가 대기시간을 줄일 수 있지만, 패스트트랙이 평가 자체의 면제나 전력 공급 확보를 의미하지는 않는다.

articles.title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.
articles.summary: HardwareDx는 그래프 기반 파운데이션 모델로 여러 하드웨어 플랫폼의 고장을 진단하는 데이터센터 유지보수 시스템이다. 연구진은 Google의 실제 운영 환경에서 GPU 플랫폼 가동 중단 시간을 18.3%, TPU 플랫폼은 16.1% 줄였다고 보고했다. 신규 하드웨어 품질보증 시간도 각각 28.3%와 25.1% 단축돼, 단일 모델을 통한 다종 장비 진단과 도입 효율 개선을 보여준다. 대규모 AI 학습 인프라의 장애 비용을 낮출 가능성이 있으나, 다른 운영 환경에서도 같은 효과가 나타나는지는 별도 검증이 필요하다.

articles.title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
articles.content: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API, a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency, and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. What is the Perplexity Orchestrator API? The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI. It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1. Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator, without /v1. Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. How does provider failover work? Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: Triggers are provider errors, rate limits and timeouts. Each attempt has a time-to-first-token limit and a total-duration limit. The values are not published. Invalid or over-context requests return HTTP 400 and are not retried. If every deployment fails, the API returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Requests that fail before producing output are not billed. You cannot pick a deployment yourself. What do the reliability and speed numbers show? Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. How does automatic routing with perplexity/auto work? Routing is in preview. You set model to perplexity/auto and pass a routing object. It holds a default_model and 1 to 5 routes, each with a name, description and model. A decision model reads the conversation and route descriptions. It never sees route names or model IDs. If nothing matches, or the decision model fails or times out, the default model answers. So do media inputs. Response headers report the result: x-perplexity-autoroute-outcome, -route and -confidence. The default policy sends traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, with simple requests going to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity also lists built-in Lower cost, Balanced and Higher quality profiles, plus an Auto effort preview. && Can routing work around refusals? Perplexity tested this on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1, run in Claude Code. Anthropic documents that Claude Fable 5.2 safeguards can block benign security and life sciences work. Claude Fable 5.2 alone: 38/63 tasks. Fable plus routes to GPT-6.1 Sol: 41/63. Fable plus routes to GPT-6 Astra: 41/63. The routes covered security, biology and after_refusal requests. That is +3 tasks, at a higher estimated cost per task. Perplexity calls it an adjusted comparison; results vary by workload. How is Orchestrator priced? Each request is billed at the answering model’s published per-token rate. Failover to another provider does not change the rate. Perplexity says there is no additional platform fee on top of credits. For example, perplexity/glm-5.3 lists $1.4 input, $4.4 output and $0.26 cache read per 1M tokens. Usage draws from prepaid Perplexity API credits, also purchasable through AWS Marketplace. Access is tiered by cumulative credit purchases: Tier 0: Google, xAI and open-weight models. Tier 1 ($50): OpenAI and most Anthropic models. Tier 2 ($250): Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5 and the Fable models. How does it compare with OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway? articles.summary: Perplexity가 여러 프런티어·공개 가중치 모델을 단일 엔드포인트와 통합 결제로 제공하는 Orchestrator API를 출시했다고 보도됐다. OpenAI Chat Completions·Responses와 Anthropic Messages 요청 형식을 지원하며, 제공업체 오류·호출 제한·시간 초과가 발생하면 모델은 유지한 채 다른 배포 제공업체로 전환한다. 잘못된 요청은 재시도하지 않고 개발자가 배포처를 직접 지정할 수 없다는 제약이 있다. 회사는 자체 운영 트래픽에서 신뢰도 개선을 보고했지만 구체적인 성공률은 공개하지 않아, 통합 편의성과 장애 대응 효과를 도입 환경에서 확인할 필요가 있다.

articles.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
articles.summary: QDA는 에이전트가 모델과 정밀도에 맞는 학습 후 양자화 조합을 설계하고 평가하는 폐쇄루프 시스템이다. 원본 모델과의 출력 KL 발산으로 후보를 빠르게 선별한 뒤 긴 생성으로 반복 루프 등의 실패를 점검하며, 호환 가능한 양자화 기법 라이브러리를 활용한다. 연구진은 네 추론 모델에서 최강 공개 조합 대비 평균 정확도를 정밀도별로 0.9~2.2%포인트 높였고, 320B MoE 모델의 W4A4 설정에서는 FP8 기준 정확도의 98.3%를 유지했다고 보고했다. 탐색당 64 GPU시간이 필요하지만 기존 서빙 커널에서 추가 추론 오버헤드 없이 동작하며, 라이브러리와 평가 도구는 공개 예정이라고 밝혔다.

articles.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 언어모델 안에 별도의 제3자 관찰자 역할을 학습시켜, 모델 자신의 행동에 관한 질문에 검증 가능한 답을 하도록 하는 내성적 감독 방식을 제안한다. Qwen3.6-27B 기반 관찰자는 학습에 사용하지 않은 다섯 감독 평가에서 평균 AUROC 0.907을 기록해 정직성 학습·출력 기록 감시·활성값 기반 방법을 앞섰다. 관찰자 학습 뒤에는 다른 감시 방법들도 평균적으로 개선돼, 감독 가능한 행동 특성을 모델에 학습시키는 접근의 가능성을 보여준다. 다만 이 결과가 평가 범위를 넘어 모든 기만이나 보상 해킹을 탐지한다는 의미는 아니다.

articles.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23750v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.
articles.summary: LED는 확산 언어모델의 수정 연산을 토큰 교체에서 삽입·삭제까지 확장하는 후속 학습 프레임워크다. 최장 공통 부분수열 정렬로 수정 지도 신호를 자동 생성하고, 이전 단계의 오류를 다음 단계에서 고치도록 다단계 학습을 수행한다. LLaDA2.1-Mini Base 16B에 적용했을 때 신뢰도 기반 디코딩의 12개 벤치마크 평균 점수는 54.86에서 57.10으로, 순전파당 토큰 수는 6.14에서 7.05로 증가했다. 누락·잉여 토큰으로 인한 연쇄 오류를 다루는 데 유용한 접근이지만, 제시된 효율 지표가 곧바로 실제 서비스 지연시간 개선을 뜻하지는 않는다.

articles.title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
articles.summary: Chorus는 짧은 토큰 연속열을 저장하는 n-그램 임베딩 테이블을 네트워크 전체가 공유하면서, 각 층이 현재 은닉 상태에 따라 서로 다르게 읽도록 하는 구조다. 연구진은 테이블 파라미터 12억 개로 96억 개를 사용하는 FactorEngram과 Engram보다 나은 텍스트 예측 성능을 얻어, 유사 품질에 필요한 테이블 크기를 87% 줄였다고 보고했다. Ember 옵티마이저와 결합하면 AdamW 대비 테이블 옵티마이저 메모리를 99.2% 줄이면서 학습 성능을 유지했다. 대규모 외부 임베딩 용량을 활용하는 언어모델의 메모리 부담을 낮추는 결과이며, 절감률은 전체 모델 메모리가 아닌 해당 구성요소 기준이다.

articles.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.23480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.
articles.summary: 응급 CT·MRI 100건을 대상으로 여섯 시각언어모델을 평가한 후향적 연구에서, 자유롭게 영상을 탐색하는 조건의 진단 정확도는 32.6%였다. 모든 절편이나 핵심 절편을 한 번에 제공하면 정확도가 약 42%로 높아졌지만, 영상의학과 전문의가 함께 판독한 30건에서는 자유 탐색 모델 30.0%와 전문의 77.0%의 큰 격차가 나타났다. 모델은 초기에 세운 가설을 유지하는 경향이 강했고, 최종 답변의 중앙 신뢰도는 90%였으나 실제 정답률은 38.9%였다. 제한된 공개 사례 평가이지만, 자율 영상 탐색과 높은 자기 확신을 임상적 신뢰성으로 간주해서는 안 된다는 근거를 제공한다.

articles.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
articles.content: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.
articles.summary: RSIBench-Infra는 에이전트가 학습·추론 인프라 전체를 최적화할 수 있는지 평가하는 20개 과제의 벤치마크다. NVIDIA GPU와 Ascend NPU에서 최대 32개 가속기를 사용하는 구성을 포함하고, 에이전트가 엔진·커널·명령어 수준을 수정하도록 허용한다. 독립 평가에서 전체 과제 결과의 66.2%가 품질 제약을 충족하면서 1.10배를 넘는 속도 향상을 달성했다. 개별 커널 개선이 아닌 종단간 성능과 재현 가능한 배포를 평가한다는 의미가 있으며, 일관된 최적화 성공은 여전히 과제로 남았다.

articles.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
articles.content: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.
articles.summary: BubbleTea는 MoE 모델 서빙에서 전문가별 토큰 배분 불균형으로 생기는 GPU 유휴 시간을 미세조정에 활용하는 시스템이다. 각 층의 라우팅 결과로 GPU별 대기 구간을 예측하고, 이미 적재된 가중치를 재사용하는 짧은 학습 작업을 배치한다. A100 네 장과 세 MoE 모델을 사용한 평가에서 기존 동시 실행 시스템 LLMStation보다 미세조정 처리량이 1.9~6.2배 높았다. 버스트형 운영 트래픽에서는 단독 서빙 대비 p90 지연시간 증가를 7% 이내로 유지하면서 학습을 3.3배 빠르게 수행했지만, 모든 평가 작업에서 동일한 지연 제약을 만족한 것은 아니다.

articles.title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench
articles.content: Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory, a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6, a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200. Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. && How does it compare with ALMA, MemEvolve and Harness-Zero? Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. articles.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode
articles.content: SID AI has released SID-2, its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. TL;DR Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models). Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai, plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries. Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested. Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG, above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704. Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG, 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet. What is SID-2 and how does it work? SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again. Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required, since SID-2 only sees what your tools return. SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one. What are reasoning effort and Metric Steering? SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. How was SID-2 trained? Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup. How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks? SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report. SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s. SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s. SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table. Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287. Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs. && SID-2 vs GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5 FeatureSID-2 (medium)SID-2 Swarm (6 agents)GPT-6 Astra (max)Claude Opus 5.5 (medium)TypeAgentic search modelMulti-agent searchGeneral LLMGeneral LLMParametersNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedContext262k (report) / 256k (site)Effectively infinite (per SID)Not disclosed1MNDCG, SID benchmark0.5850.7010.7040.577Inference time per query3.11 s17.7 s135 s25.1 sCost per 1,000 queries$6.54$263$2,141$131API price (input / output per 1M)$0.25 / $1.00$0.50 / $2.00$10 / $50$4 / $20 NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded. How can developers deploy SID-2? SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten. SDKs exist for Python (sid-sdk), TypeScript (@sid-ai/sid-sdk) and Go (github.com/sidhq/sid-go). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format. articles.title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.24055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.
articles.summary: LexTemporis는 LLM이 작성한 법률 판단 프로그램을 평가자의 법 해석이 아니라 한국 상장기업이 공시한 10,901개 기업·연도별 중소기업 지위 기록과 비교한다. 연구에서는 하나의 경과규정을 반영하는 것만으로 공시 기록과의 일치율이 83~86%에서 89~90%로 상승했다. 네 LLM을 대상으로 한 사전등록 비교에서는 모든 모델에 일관되게 우수한 법령 제공 조건이 없었고, 평가자의 해석을 정답으로 삼으면 실제 기록 대비 성능을 과장할 수 있었다. 국내 법률 자동화에서 시행 시점·경과조치와 독립적인 결과 기록을 함께 검증해야 한다는 실무적 시사점을 제공한다.

articles.title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
articles.content: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 현장 로봇과 환경 모니터링의 시각 검사를 제한된 연산·센싱 예산 아래 관측 순서를 계획하는 문제로 다룬다. 소형 순환 월드모델과 명시적인 실행 제약을 결합해 클래스 질의·이미지 자르기·보정·중단을 다단계 탐색으로 결정하며, 기존 검출기는 재학습하지 않는다. 지상·광학·소나 등 여덟 벤치마크에서 정적 우선순위 방식 대비 AP가 최대 28.4%포인트 개선됐고 계획 비용은 11밀리초로 보고됐다. 제한된 호출 예산에서 검사 효율을 높일 가능성이 있지만, 개선 폭은 데이터셋과 비용 조건에 따라 달랐다.

articles.title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence
articles.content: An LLM presents you a wrong value extracted from a document as fact. That error is costly, especially when basing decisions on it. The Nutrient Data Extraction API targets that problem. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown. Extract maps fields from a document onto your JSON schema, and split, classify and form endpoints provide useful primitives for your document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient (formerly PSPDFKit) runs the same engine behind an MCP server, agent skill, Mac app and SDK. TL;DR Size: A hosted API with 4 parse modes plus auto routing. Runs on: Nutrient cloud, your own servers via SDK, or an Apple silicon Mac. Where to try it: Studio, a browser workspace to configure and test parsing, extraction,classification, splitting, and form filling. Performance: 86.2 overall on Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench, top of 19 settings (live API, Agentic). Best: 86.2 at 1.8¢ per page, versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting. How do you test it in Studio before writing code? Studio is Nutrient’s browser workspace for configuring and testing the API before integrating it in your application. It enables you to test parsing, extraction, classification, splitting, and form filling on your own files. A typical loop: Upload a sample document and set the parameters you plan to send. Draft a schema in the UI, or generate one based on your own documents. Run it on a fresh document, then inspect values and citations. Save the setup as a versioned preset. The API calls it a processor, with a proc_ ID. Score preset versions against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set. Processors saved in Studio can then be called from the API by ID. Which mode should you pick? Auto routes each page to structure, understand or agentic. If the mode is omitted, the API defaults to understand. Extract adds $0.006 per page. **API docs list text-mode extract; the agent skill starts at structure. Pricing is in dollars, from 1 balance shared across Nutrient’s cloud APIs, so teams can mix and match. The free plan gives you $5 monthly usage that covers about 330 understand-mode extractions. Starter costs $75 a month for $90 of usage; Growth costs $275 for $345. How does grounded confidence work? In Nutrient’s confidence post, a field scored 0.97 but came from the wrong column. The current score is a composite of optional signals: token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format. Nutrient’s NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field. When no score exists, confidence is omitted, not low. Each field also gets a match label: id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found. Gate on the label first, then confidence. Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browserimport json, requests API_KEY = "your_api_key" schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "invoice_number": {"type": "string", "description": "Invoice number below the supplier details."}, "total_amount": {"type": "number", "description": "Printed final total including tax. Not the subtotal."}, }, "required": ["invoice_number", "total_amount"], } instructions = {"schema": schema, "parseConfig": {"mode": "understand"}, "options": {"includeCitations": True}} with open("invoice.pdf", "rb") as f: r = requests.post( "https://api.nutrient.io/extraction/extract", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}, files={"file": ("invoice.pdf", f, "application/pdf"), "instructions": (None, json.dumps(instructions), "application/json")}, timeout=300, ) r.raise_for_status() out = r.json()["output"] data, metadata = out.get("data") or {}, out.get("metadata") or {} EXACT = {"id_match", "id_match_multiblock"} THRESHOLD = 0.97 # illustrative only; evaluate on representative documents for field in schema["properties"]: # loop over expected fields so none skip review value = data.get(field) meta = metadata.get(field) or {} match, conf = meta.get("match"), meta.get("confidence") # None = no score passes = (value is not None and match in EXACT and conf is not None and conf >= THRESHOLD) print(field, value, match, conf, "page", meta.get("pageNumber"), "PASSES_BASIC_CHECKS" if passes else "REVIEW") This demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks. The 0.97 bar mirrors money fields in Nutrient’s mortgage tutorial. How do classify and split work? A document decision model powers classify and split. Nutrient reports 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI’s Jev. How do agents use it? The hosted MCP server needs no API key. Claude Code connects with 1 command: Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browserclaude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp Claude and Codex also work via OAuth. Default agentic mode costs $0.018 per page to parse. Coding agents can install the document-extraction-api skill with npx skills add pspdfkit-labs/nutrient-skills –skill document-extraction-api. Can it run locally? On the Mac app, documents stay local only with a local model. Fully offline production needs the SDK. How does it score on WholeDoc Bench? Nutrient’s new WholeDoc Bench scores whole documents, not single pages: 480 documents, 30+ languages, 7 areas. Cross-page continuity is the biggest gap. On 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole. Nutrient built and ran it, and the main test set is private. The code is Apache-2.0, with a 10-document public sample.  Key Takeaways Fields carry pages, regions, match labels and, when available, confidence. Configure and test in Studio before writing any API code. Understand-mode extraction costs $15 per 1,000 pages. Agentic tops Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench at 86.2 for 1.8¢ per page. Charts remain hard: 64.5 is the best WholeDoc chart score. See the Data Extraction API, benchmarks, MCP server and agent skill on GitHub.
